content.title: About
content.content: The non‑citrus carbonated fruit juice drink is a refreshing beverage made from fruit juices without any citrus flavors. It offers a mild sweetness, gentle carbonation, and a bright fruit taste that appeals to a wide range of consumers.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The drink is produced from concentrates of various fruits such as apple, pear, and grape.
Absence of citrus makes it suitable for people with citrus allergies.
Carbonation is achieved by adding food‑grade carbon dioxide, giving the drink its characteristic fizz.
Natural flavorings and a modest amount of sugar or sugar substitutes are often included.
The beverage can be used in cocktails and mixers without risking flavor clashes with citrus ingredients.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: The fruit juices used in the drink contain vitamins B1, B2, and B6, which support energy metabolism.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: With a high water content, the drink helps maintain the body’s fluid balance.

items.title: Low acidity
items.content: The lack of citrus results in lower acidity, which may be gentler on sensitive stomachs.

items.title: Antioxidant compounds
items.content: Fruit extracts are rich in polyphenols that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Digestive support
items.content: Mild carbonation can promote a feeling of lightness after meals.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Some versions may contain significant amounts of sugar, which should be considered by people with diabetes or weight concerns.

items.title: Carbonation
items.content: Consuming large quantities of carbonated drinks can cause bloating or discomfort in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Fruit allergies
items.content: Individuals may be allergic to specific fruits used in the formulation.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: Preservatives may be added to extend shelf life, which are not suitable for all consumers.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Serve chilled as a standalone refreshing drink or as a base for non‑alcoholic cocktails. Adding a slice of fresh fruit can enhance the aroma.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep refrigerated and consume within 3–5 days.

pizza-with-meat-other-than-pepperoni-fro.title: Pizza with meat (not pepperoni), school lunch, thin crust

content.title: About
content.content: A pizza topped with meat but without pepperoni is a common offering in school cafeterias as a quick and filling lunch. The thin crust (3416) provides a crisp base, while meat pieces such as chicken, beef, or ham add protein. The pizza typically includes tomato sauce, mozzarella cheese, and a modest amount of vegetables.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Thin crust requires a higher baking temperature, resulting in a crunchy edge.
In school menus pizza is often considered a "fast" dish, but it can be enriched with vegetables for a more balanced meal.
Meat used in school pizzas is usually pre‑cooked (boiled or baked) to ensure food safety.
Tomato sauce is rich in lycopene, which becomes more bioavailable after heating.
Pizza is traditionally cut into triangular slices, making it easy to serve in a cafeteria.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: The meat topping provides high‑quality protein essential for growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Calcium source
items.content: Mozzarella cheese supplies calcium important for bone and teeth health.

items.title: Lycopene in sauce
items.content: Cooked tomatoes increase the availability of lycopene, a powerful antioxidant.

items.title: Energy dense
items.content: The crust delivers quick‑acting carbohydrates for immediate energy.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Meat and, when used, whole‑grain crust provide B1, B2, B6 vitamins that support metabolism.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Cheese and prepared sauce can contain a lot of salt, which is a concern for hypertension.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Traditional cheese and meat may raise saturated fat intake, relevant for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Allergens
items.content: Dairy and gluten in the crust can trigger allergic reactions.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Pizza can be high in calories, so portion control is advisable, especially for children.

items.title: Meat quality control
items.content: Improper storage or insufficient cooking of meat can lead to foodborne illness.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the pizza hot, sliced into triangles. It can be complemented with fresh vegetables (tomatoes, cucumbers) or herbs to boost nutrition. For a healthier option, choose a whole‑grain thin crust.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2 days. Reheat in an oven or microwave to restore crispness. Discard if the pizza develops a sour smell or visible mold.

content.title: About
content.content: Carnitas are a traditional Mexican dish of slowly braised pork seasoned with spices, lime, and orange juice. The meat is cooked until tender, then crisped to a golden crust, delivering a savory, slightly sweet flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The name comes from the Spanish word “carnitas,” meaning “little pieces of meat.”
Traditionally the dish is cooked in large copper pots called “cazos.”
In Mexico carnitas are commonly served in tacos, burritos, and with salsa.
Pork shoulder or butt, rich in connective tissue, is usually used to keep the meat juicy.
Carnitas are often topped with fresh cilantro, onion, and lime.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Pork provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Source of vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 supports the nervous system and red blood cell formation.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Iron from pork helps transport oxygen throughout the body.

items.title: Provides zinc
items.content: Zinc is important for immune function and wound healing.

items.title: Contains vitamin B6
items.content: Vitamin B6 participates in amino‑acid metabolism and neurotransmitter synthesis.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: Carnitas are made from fatty cuts; those monitoring fat intake should consume them in moderation.

items.title: Sodium levels
items.content: Added soy sauce or salt can raise sodium, which may be a concern for people with hypertension.

items.title: Foodborne illness risk
items.content: Undercooked pork may harbor pathogens; ensure internal temperature reaches at least 71 °C (160 °F).

items.title: Pork allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to pork.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve carnitas in soft corn or flour tortillas, topped with fresh onion, cilantro, guacamole, salsa, and a squeeze of lime. It can also be used as a filling for burritos, salads, or enjoyed as a main dish with rice and beans.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked carnitas in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in portion‑sized bags for up to 2 months. Reheat thoroughly before serving.

rice-brown-and-wild-cooked-ns-as-to-fat.title: Brown and Wild Rice, Cooked, No Salt

content.title: About
content.content: Brown and wild rice is a blend of whole‑grain brown rice and wild rice grains, cooked by steaming or boiling without added salt. It has a nutty aroma, slightly chewy texture, and a high dietary fiber content.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Wild rice is not a true rice; it belongs to the water‑grass family.
The blend is popular in low‑glycemic diets because it raises blood sugar more slowly than white rice.
Cooking retains more B‑vitamins and minerals than polishing white rice.
Wild rice contains more protein than most common rice varieties.
Combining the two grains enhances flavor complexity and texture.

items.title: Rich in fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestive health and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Source of plant protein
items.content: The blend provides about 5 g of protein per 100 g, beneficial for vegetarians.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Helps stabilize blood glucose levels, useful for people with pre‑diabetes.

items.title: Contains magnesium and phosphorus
items.content: These minerals are essential for muscle function, nerve signaling, and bone health.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Phytonutrients such as phenolic acids protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Cereal allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to rice.

items.title: Arsenic content
items.content: Wild rice can accumulate arsenic from soil; varied diet is recommended.

items.title: High phytic acid
items.content: Phytic acid may reduce mineral absorption when consumed in excess.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cooked brown and wild rice works as a side dish, a base for salads, soups, and Buddha bowls. Add it to vegetable stews, use in casseroles, or serve with yogurt‑based sauces.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked rice in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 4‑5 days. For longer storage, freeze in portions for up to 3 months.

rice-white-with-vegetables-soy-based-sau.title: White Rice with Vegetables and Soy Sauce

content.title: About
content.content: White rice with vegetables and soy sauce is a ready‑to‑eat dish that combines boiled white rice, a mix of fresh vegetables (carrot, peas, corn) and a soy‑based sauce made from soybeans. The dish is rich in carbohydrates, provides a modest amount of protein, and contains virtually no fat.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: White rice is a staple source of energy in many cultures worldwide.
Soy sauce gives the dish its characteristic umami flavor and adds a small amount of sodium.
The vegetables retain part of their vitamins and minerals thanks to quick heat treatment.
Traditionally served hot in Asian cuisine as a side or a complete meal.
The recipe can be adapted for dietary needs by using low‑sodium soy sauce.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Rice provides a rapid source of glucose, essential for maintaining energy levels.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals from vegetables
items.content: The vegetable mix adds vitamin A, vitamin C, folate, and potassium, supporting immunity and cellular function.

items.title: Low fat content
items.content: The dish is virtually fat‑free, making it suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Rich in carbohydrates
items.content: Carbohydrates from rice help replenish glycogen stores after physical activity.

items.title: Bioactive compounds in soy sauce
items.content: Soy sauce contains isoflavones that may have antioxidant properties.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Soy sauce can be high in salt; individuals monitoring sodium intake should choose reduced‑sodium versions.

items.title: Soy allergy
items.content: Some people may experience allergic reactions to soy products.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: White rice has a high glycemic index, which can cause rapid blood sugar spikes.

items.title: Low fiber
items.content: Compared to whole‑grain alternatives, white rice provides little dietary fiber.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot as a standalone meal or as a side to meat or fish dishes. Garnish with fresh green onions, sesame seeds, or a squeeze of lime to enhance flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared dish in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Reheat in a microwave or skillet, adding a splash of water to prevent drying out.
